name: paperkey
desc: Extract just secret information out of OpenPGP secret keys
why: Strips an OpenPGP secret key down to its raw secret bytes for paper backup, a neat dissection of a file format.

brief.what_it_is: Paperkey is a command-line tool that takes an OpenPGP secret key (GnuPG, PGP, etc.) and strips it down to just the secret bytes, printing them as text or raw output for a paper backup. Going the other way, it takes those printed or re-entered bytes plus the matching public key and rebuilds the full secret key file. It is a single C program distributed as a tarball, with a Win32 binary also offered.
brief.why_it_exists: David Shaw's framing is that paper is a durable 'if-all-else-fails' backup for keys, since CD-Rs, tapes and drives often lose data within years. A full secret key file is much larger than its secret parts because it includes a complete copy of the public key, and the public key is widely available on keyservers, so only the secret portion needs archiving.
brief.how_it_works: Paperkey parses the OpenPGP packet structure and keeps only the secret key material plus minor packet structure, which the author says is about 149 bytes for a DSA+Elgamal key that was 1281 bytes whole. Restoring requires the public key file; paperkey combines it with the pasted-in secret bytes to produce a secret key. It does no cryptography itself, and any passphrase on the original key carries over unchanged. Output can be base16 (human-readable, default width 78) or raw, and it includes a CRC check that can be overridden with --ignore-crc-error.

commands_seen.context: Extracts the secret data from the key file into a text file meant for printing.
Restore: combines the public keyring with the printed secret data to rebuild the secret key file.
Pipes an exported secret key through paperkey straight to the printer, since stdin is used when --secret-key is absent.

brief.install_notes: Not covered by the homepage beyond the tarball and Win32 zip downloads, each with a detached OpenPGP signature from the author's key 0x99242560. Building from the POSIX tarball is the standard route. A RPM spec file is included; the README-style instructions say to build with rpmbuild -ta /path/to/the/paperkey/tarball.tar.gz. No account or runtime is needed beyond the binary. The author recommends test-restoring the key before filing the paper away.
brief.standout: The project's clever observation is that the secret part of a key is tiny compared to the whole file, so a key can be reduced to a few hundred bytes of text you can retype, which makes a paper backup practical. Its honest framing that paper is not a secure store and that it adds no crypto is also unusual for a security-adjacent tool.
brief.status: quiet. The homepage shows version 1.6 with a copyright range of 2007-2018, and says earlier releases and 'the usual GitHub stuff' are on GitHub, but the page gives no release date or recent-activity signal and I did not check GitHub. Treat as unknown beyond 'not recently announced'.
brief.caveats: Output is a paper backup, not secure storage; the page stresses it is for last-resort restore only. Any passphrase on the original key carries over unchanged. Reconstruction needs the public key as well. Restored text must be re-entered accurately, by hand, OCR or QR, and a CRC error stops restore unless you pass --ignore-crc-error. Build and install details beyond the tarball are thin on this page. The Win32 binary is a precompiled download. The licence is not stated on the homepage.
quotes: The goal with paper is not secure storage.
In fact, paperkey doesn't do any crypto at all, but just saves and restores the original secret key, whether it is encrypted or not.
It's a lot easier to re-enter 149 bytes correctly.
